clue.text: Strange boy does marry an important person

indicators.note: something strange is out of the ordinary, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: M is the standard abbreviation for married, used here for marry

explanation.surface: An odd lad weds a dignitary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' shuffles BOY and DOES together with M (from 'marry') to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a big name is the same as saying they matter: a person of standing or consequence.

clue.text: Stage alchemist

parts.note: the swindling alchemist of Ben Jonson's play The Alchemist, whose name is also an adjective for crafty or finely drawn

explanation.surface: A theatrical character who turns lead into gold.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben Jonson's comedy The Alchemist (1610) centres on a conman-alchemist whose name is an ordinary English adjective meaning cunning.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective meaning artful or cunning is the name Jonson gave his trickster alchemist on the stage.

clue.text: Place where a convict entered Military Academy

indicators.note: one piece going into another means the letters sit inside the outer piece

parts.note: an old lag is slang for a convict

explanation.surface: A prisoner turned up at a military college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entered' is the container signal; an old lag is British slang for a habitual prisoner.
explanation.definitionFit: Malaga is a port city in southern Spain, so it is a named place.

clue.text: Caught between lake and rock, in battle

indicators.note: the caught letter is set between the lake and the rock pieces

parts.note: Bala Lake (Llyn Tegid) is the largest natural lake in Wales
lava is molten rock that hardens into stone
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: Someone is trapped between water and stone during a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'between' places the cricket abbreviation for caught amid a Welsh lake and molten rock. The Battle of Balaclava (1854) was fought in the Crimean War.
explanation.definitionFit: Balaclava was a Crimean War engagement famous for the Charge of the Light Brigade.

clue.text: Lack of submission with bedside I once left in disarray

indicators.note: things left in disarray are jumbled up, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to obey and leaves the bedroom in a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left in disarray' jumbles BEDSIDE, I and ONCE (12 letters) into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Refusing to obey is a failure to submit to authority.

clue.text: An old person is a blunderer

definitions.meaning: an archaic or dialect word for an elderly man, also a boss
one who makes gaffes, that is social blunders

explanation.definitionFit: The word is old slang for an elderly man, and can also be read as someone making faux pas or slips.

clue.text: Unfortunately a shortage

parts.note: a lack is a shortage of something

explanation.surface: Sadly, there is not enough.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic exclamation of sorrow, used like 'alas' to mean sadly.

clue.text: Fine hall made by peasants

indicators.note: the letters are made into something new, so the words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Farm workers built a grand hall.
explanation.definitionFit: Fellahin are agricultural labourers in Egypt and Arabic-speaking countries.

clue.text: Give out afresh what a king does, without a fool

indicators.note: in the old sense of outside, so the king's action wraps around the fool

parts.note: a king reigns, the verb here in its base form

explanation.surface: A monarch hands out duties again, having dismissed his jester.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking' but here means 'outside', its old sense: the king's verb wraps around the fool.
explanation.definitionFit: To allot again is to hand out a task or role once more.

clue.text: Without a band thrash not so much

parts.note: to belt someone is to thrash them

explanation.surface: An unbelted figure takes a beating, though a lighter one.
explanation.definitionFit: A belt is a band worn round the waist, so lacking one is to be without it.

clue.text: Plant in which trouble had returned

indicators.note: something returned goes back, so the letters are read in reverse

explanation.surface: A garden flower that has caused problems again.
explanation.definitionFit: The dahlia is a tuberous garden flower from Mexico.

clue.text: Canals and trains run differently for Northerners

indicators.note: if they run differently the letters take a new course, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Waterways and railways operate in contrasting ways for people in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'run differently' rearranges CANALS and TRAINS. Lancashire is a county in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: People from Lancashire, a county in north-west England, are from the north of the country.

clue.text: Reason puts soldier in place

indicators.note: one piece is put in the other

explanation.surface: Common sense locates a serviceman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is the container signal; loc. is the abbreviation for location, as in loc. cit.
explanation.definitionFit: Logic is sound reasoning, so it stands for reason.

clue.text: Judges used to have them and they have beaks

definitions.meaning: British judges put on a black cap to pass a death sentence
small songbirds of the warbler family, with beaks like any bird

explanation.definitionFit: The black square worn when sentencing to death, and also warblers named for their dark crowns.

clue.text: Picking for the team behind a worker and me is damaging

indicators.note: the team-picking piece comes after the worker and me pieces

parts.note: a hand is a worker, as in farmhand
a player picked for a national team is capped

explanation.surface: Choosing players after consulting a worker and me is harmful to the side.
explanation.walkthrough: To cap is to select a player for a national side, awarding a cap.
explanation.definitionFit: Handicapping places someone at a disadvantage, so it hurts or hinders them.

clue.text: Walk which could make one damper

indicators.note: the letters could be made into a new word, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A stroll in the rain would leave someone wetter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could make' rearranges ONE and DAMPER (9 letters).
explanation.definitionFit: A promenade is a leisurely stroll, often along a seafront.

clue.text: Ask Europe for food

annotationWithheld.why: Ask Europe for food (8): SEEDCAKE looks like an anagram of ASKED + EEC, but 'Ask' gives no D and no word signals an anagram; the printed clue looks garbled

clue.text: Performer of dangerous feats has to check a person

parts.note: to stunt growth is to check it

explanation.surface: A daredevil must hold back someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A double who does risky action scenes in film performs dangerous feats.

clue.text: Additional variant for interest in the external world

explanation.surface: Another form of something is offered for outward-looking people.
explanation.definitionFit: Jung's term for an outward-turning personality, focused on people and things outside the self.

clue.text: Graduate account held by us — calculator needed

indicators.note: one piece is held by another, so it sits inside it

parts.note: BA is a Bachelor of Arts

explanation.surface: An arts graduate's bookkeeping requires a counting device.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held by' puts the graduate inside the account abbreviation; 'needed' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: An abacus is a frame of beads used for counting and arithmetic.

clue.text: Queen follows times for destroyer

indicators.note: the queen piece comes after the times piece

explanation.surface: A monarch comes after ages of a warship.
explanation.walkthrough: ER (Elizabeth Regina) is the crossword Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that rubs out pencil marks wipes them out, a destroyer of writing.

clue.text: Informer against a small weight right behind the study

indicators.note: the weight and right pieces come after the study piece

parts.note: a den is a private study
an ounce is a small weight

explanation.surface: A snitch weighing little stands right behind the study.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who publicly accuses or informs on others speaks out against them.

clue.text: Anglo-Saxon brought in to annul riches

indicators.note: letters brought in within the phrase sit inside it, spanning the words

explanation.surface: An Old English figure is brought in to cancel wealth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought in' signals the name inside 'annUL RICHes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulric is an Old English personal name, borne by Anglo-Saxons.

clue.text: Decoration sported by the Queen is something that glows

indicators.note: a decoration sported by someone is worn on them, so it goes inside

parts.note: MBE is a British honour, Member of the Order of the British Empire

explanation.surface: The monarch wears a medal that shines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sported by' means worn by, so the British honour goes inside the royal cipher.
explanation.definitionFit: A glowing remnant of coal or wood in a dying fire.

clue.text: Fall for the mud following publicity

indicators.note: the mud piece comes after the publicity piece

explanation.surface: Someone is taken in by muck that comes after advertising.
explanation.definitionFit: To be smitten with or think highly of someone is to fall for them.

clue.text: Scientific instruments can get broken in bundles

indicators.note: one piece is put in the other
if they get broken the letters are smashed and rearranged

explanation.surface: Lab equipment can be damaged when packed in bundles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get broken' signals the anagram of the word can, and 'in' puts the result inside the bundles.
explanation.definitionFit: Laboratory scales used for weighing precisely.

clue.text: She starts well in Greek and has a fine finish

parts.note: eu is the Greek for well, as in euphoria

explanation.surface: A woman begins well in Greek and ends finely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts' and 'finish' just place the pieces at the start and end.
explanation.definitionFit: Eunice is a woman's name, so it can stand for 'she'.

clue.text: Judger of mixed roses beside a fool

indicators.note: the anagram piece sits next to the fool piece
mixed letters are jumbled, so roses is rearranged

explanation.surface: An evaluator of mixed flowers stands next to a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: An assessor evaluates or judges value, as for tax or insurance.
